desc:
Split the positive integer n into at least two positive integers that add up to n. Return the largest product the parts can have.

n = 2  -> 1    (1 + 1)
n = 6  -> 9    (3 + 3)
n = 10 -> 36   (3 + 3 + 4)
hints: Try small n by hand: 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7. Which part sizes keep showing up in the best splits?
Look at the first part j that you take off. The rest, n - j, is either kept whole or itself split further, so you can multiply j by max(n - j, best[n - j]).

Compute best[i] for i = 2..n with best[i] = max over 1 ≤ j < i of j * max(i - j, best[i - j]). Notice that this is an unbounded knapsack where the weights are the part sizes and the 'value' is a product.
editorial: Let best[i] be the largest product of a split of i into at least two parts. Take the first part j (with 1 ≤ j < i). What remains is i - j, and the remaining part may either stay as a single number, contributing i - j, or be split further, contributing best[i - j]. Hence best[i] = max(j * max(i - j, best[i - j])) over all j. The small cases best[2] = 1 and best[3] = 2 start the table. The table takes O(n²) time.

The table also reveals the pattern behind the closed form: an optimal split consists of 3s, plus one 2 or two 2s (or one 4) for the remainder. Parts of size 1 never help, parts of size 4 or more can be broken into 2s and 3s without losing product, and three 2s (product 8) are worse than two 3s (product 9). The range of n is capped at 58 so that the result fits in a 32-bit signed integer.
